Policy Name – Internet, Email and Social Media

Policy Number

Version Number

Scope

This policy applies to all Bagwan Health, staff, contractors, Allied Health professionals, Credentialed Specialists, volunteers and students.

Policy

This policy defines the standards and processes associated with the responsible use of internet, email and social media at Bagwan Health. This policy has been developed in conjunction with the National Code of Conduct for Health Care Workers and other relevant VIC Health and Bagwan Health policies and legislation.

Procedure 

Internet, Email and Social Media

Internet, email and social media are digital methods of communication and allow individuals and organization to communicate, find and share information, distribute resources and much more. Access to the internet at Bagwan Health is a privilege and everyone must adhere to this policy.

Internet and Email Usage

Bagwan Health staff, contractors, volunteers and students are expected to use the internet responsibly and productively. Internet access is limited to job-related activities only and personal use is not permitted. Job-related activities include research and educational tasks that can be completed using the internet that assist a person in their role.

All internet data that is composed, transmitted and/or received by Bagwan Health computer systems is considered to belong to Bagwan Health and is recognized as part of its official data. It is therefore subject to disclosure for legal reasons or to other appropriate third parties.

The equipment, services and technology used to access the internet are the property of Bagwan Health, and as such Bagwan Health reserves the right to monitor internet traffic and monitor and access data that is composed, sent or received through its online connections.

Emails sent via the company email system should not contain content that is deemed to be offensive. This includes, though is not restricted to, the use of vulgar or harassing language/images.

All sites and downloads may be monitored and/or blocked by Bagwan Health if they are deemed to be harmful and/or not productive to business.

Installing Software

The installation of new software such as internet browsers or instant messaging technology is strictly prohibited. If there is a requirement for new software to be installed, a request must be made via the I.T. portal on the intranet home page. All requests must be approved prior to installation by the relevant manager and the I.T. Manager.

 

What is Unacceptable Use of Internet and Email?

 

Unacceptable use of the internet or email includes, but is not limited to:

·         Sending or posting discriminatory, harassing, or threatening messages or images on the internet or via Bagwan Health’s email service

·         Using computers to perpetrate fraud, and/or software, film or music piracy

·         Stealing, using, or disclosing someone else’s password without authorization

·         Downloading, copying or pirating software and electronic files that are copyrighted or without authorization

·         Sharing confidential material or proprietary information outside of the organization

·         Hacking into unauthorized websites

·         Sending or posting information that is defamatory to the company, its products/services, colleagues and/or customers

·         Introducing malicious software onto the company network and/or jeopardizing the security of the organization’s electronic communications systems

·         Sending or posting chain letters, solicitations, or advertisements not related to business purposes or activities

 

·         Passing off personal views as representing those of Bagwan Health

If unsure about what constitutes acceptable internet usage, then consult a manager for further guidance and clarification

Social Media

Social media is a popular communication method used to interact, share content and collaborate outside of traditional means of communication. The growing use of social media and networking sites is providing opportunities for Bagwan Health to communicate and share information. Social media is also a powerful engagement tool for Bagwan Health to communicate with staff, external stakeholders and the community. 

For the purpose of this policy, social media includes, but is not limited to:

·         Social sites/apps e.g. Facebook or Twitter

·         Business networking sites/apps e.g. LinkedIn

·         Video sharing sites/apps e.g. YouTube

·         Photo sharing sites/apps e.g. Instagram

·         Blogs e.g. WordPress

·         Forums and discussion boards e.g. Yahoo! or Google Groups

·         Podcasts e.g. Simplecast

 

·         Any other websites that allow individual users or companies to use simple publishing tools

Always remember that posts and comments made on social media, either professionally or personally, could potentially be permanent.

Bagwan Health’s Use of Social Media

Bagwan Health uses social media for the following purposes:

·         Encourage feedback from the public

·         Engage with members of the community and community groups

·         Facilitate a communication channel for the public to access information about our services

·         Facilitate a communication channel for health promotion

·         Promote Bagwan Health events

·         Facilitate a communication for public health announcements such as new programs, outbreaks

·         Provide interesting and useful information for the community

·         Engage a younger demographic

 

·         Enable information sharing for staff, contractors, volunteers, students and clinicians

Inappropriate Material for Social Media

Social media can be a fun personal platform, but it can create problems professionally, especially when inappropriate material is shared. Inappropriate material includes, but is not limited to, any material that is:

 

·         Misleading or deceiving, whether intended or not

·         Offensive, threatening, intimidating, abusive, defamatory or that may lead to criminal or civil liability

·         Discriminating against colleagues, patients/clients or the public, on the grounds of sex, pregnancy, marital status, age, race, nationality, cultural or ethnic background, religious background, disability, HIV/AIDS, sexuality

·         Victimising, harassing, vilifying or bullying

·         Potentially damaging to Bagwan Health or Bagwan Health’s reputation in the community

Information that is retained and secured by Bagwan Health, in accordance with Section 5 of the Health Records and Information Privacy Act 2002 or the Health Services Act 1997, is also inappropriate for sharing on social media.

 

This includes private health information, records, photos or images, tax file numbers, employee personal details. 

Responsibilities

All staff, contractors, volunteers and students have a responsibility to:

·         Act in accordance with this policy and any other relevant procedures and legislation when using social media

·         Report any instances of inappropriate material, comments or intellectual property being posted to their line manager or a more senior staff member

·         Carry out their duties responsibly, effectively, efficiently and in accordance to the National Code of Conduct for Health Care Workers

·         Ensure they only access and use social media sites outside working hours in a private capacity, unless for the purpose of carrying out their duties

·         Use Bagwan Health computers and network connections appropriately and in line with relevant policies.

Managers are to:

·         Ensure that staff, contractors, volunteers and students working within their area of management understand this policy

 

·         Investigate any alleged breach of the National Code of Conduct for Health Care Workers by their staff

Private Use of Social Media

Staff, contractors, volunteers and students should not expect to be able to access and use social media during working hours, unless for the purpose of carrying out their duties. The use of social for personal purposes while at work is strictly prohibited.

Outside of work hours, they should be reminded that anything they post to their personal accounts can be potentially seen by anyone with access to social media.

Staff, contractors, volunteers and students with personal social media accounts should be reminded that:

·         Anything they post on their personal accounts can potentially be seen by anyone with access to social media

·         It is their responsibility to know who their online friends/contacts are and to use privacy settings accordingly

·         Identifying or discussing their place of work in their personal comments is not allowed

·         They should not accept friend requests from former or existing patients as this can breach professional boundaries

·         Making comments or remarks about patients that have been treated at Bagwan Health may breach the Code of Conduct and break patient confidentiality

·         Inappropriate material, which may contravene any Victorian Health Policy or bring VIC Health or Bagwan Health into disrepute, should not be uploaded to personal accounts

·         They must not offer opinions or comments on behalf of Bagwan Health or imply that their comments are made as a representative of Bagwan Health, as to do so would breach the Code of Conduct. 

Violation of Internet, Email and Social Media Use Policy

 

Violation of this policy could result in disciplinary and/or legal action leading up to and including termination of employment. Staff, contractors, volunteers and students may also be held personally liable for damages caused by any violations of this policy.

Bagwan Health on Social Media

Bagwan Health social media pages, profiles and sites are developed to engage with the public. The content of the social media is intended for public use.

Any Bagwan staff member, contractor, volunteer or student who wishes to create social media sites or accounts representing Bagwan Health or any of its facilities or services must first obtain permission from their Director, followed by the Media and Communications Manager.  

 

The content on Bagwan Health social media pages, profiles and sites will be captured and archived on a regular basis in accordance with State Records Guideline – Records Management and Web 2.0.

pages.html:
Policy Name – Language Services

Policy Number

Version Number

Scope

All staff and contractors employed by Bagwan Health, Allied Health professionals, Credentialed Specialists and students should be aware of these policies and procedures and be trained in how to access and effectively use language services.

Policy 

Bagwan Health requires all interpreters or translators, whether they are Australian Institute of Interpreters and Translators (AUSIT) members or not, to adhere to the AUSIT Code of Ethics and Code of Conduct.

 

In summary, the code obliges members to:

·         Maintain professional detachment, impartiality, objectivity and confidentiality

·         Decline work beyond their competence

·         Strive for excellence through continuous regular professional development

·         Promote working conditions, relationships and an understanding of roles that facilitate collaboration and quality service delivery

 

·         Adhere to dispute resolution procedures.

This policy defines the standards and processes associated with working with interpreting and translating services. It is intended to support staff at all levels to provide quality language services to patients and thereby respond to the needs of Victoria’s diverse community, including refugees and asylum-seekers, migrants and people using sign language.

Procedure

Interpreting Services

Interpreting is a highly specialised skill involving the precise, effective and timely translation of information from one language to another. Including an interpreter in a consultation can be beneficial where the patient prefers to speak, or is more fluent, in a language other than English, or the patient’s English skills are inadequate for the consultation.

Why Engage an Interpreter?

Clear and effective communication underpins every aspect of good practice. It is linked to the patient’s satisfaction, adherence to instructions, and health outcomes. Ineffective communication can result in limited, delayed, inefficient care, leading to more costly treatment and intervention, as well as negatively impacting the patient’s understanding of, and trust in, the healthcare system at large.

Engaging interpreters has been found to:

·         Decrease communication errors

·         Increase the patient’s comprehension

·         Reduce unnecessary tests and treatments

·         Improve clinical outcomes

·         Raise the quality of care to the same level as that for people without language barriers

·         Improve the patient’s satisfaction with understanding self-care and follow-up plans, reducing errors and better adherence to treatment

·         Improve the healthcare provider’s satisfaction

Failure to determine the need for, and engage, an interpreter may be considered to be a breach in duty of care.

Informed Consent

Engaging an interpreter is essential for obtaining informed consent from patients with limited English proficiency or Deaf patients from migrant and refugee backgrounds.

Consent for any procedure requires the patient to be:

·         Fully informed about the underlying illness or disease, the nature of the procedure, the consequences of not having the procedure, the degree of certainty about the outcome, the time for recovery and the cost

·         Able to raise any concerns about the risks of particular relevance to them.

At a minimum, you should:

·         Assess the patient’s understanding of the information provided to consent to treatment, taking into consideration both the complexity of the issues and the person’s English language proficiency

·         Engage an interpreter for people with limited English language proficiency.

Consent may not be valid if it is obtained through the person’s family members, partners or friends.

Accessible Interpreter Services

Patients must be informed of the interpreting services that are available to them when accessing health care, as well as collecting medications from a pharmacist and that services are:

·         Provided by certified interpreters

·         Free for the patient

·         Confidential.

Assessing the Need for an Interpreter

Whenever possible, the need for an interpreter should be determined prior to an appointment. Assessing how well a patient understands English is the first step in identifying the need for an interpreter.

Even when a patient appears to have adequate English proficiency in an everyday conversation, stressful or unfamiliar situations may affect their ability to communicate effectively. In addition, the patient may have gaps in confidence and competence between understanding what is being said and being able to ask questions in English.

In addition, Deaf people from migrant and refugee backgrounds will require an Auslan/English interpreter (if they use Auslan) or a Deaf and Auslan/English interpreter (if they use another sign language).

You should engage an interpreter if:

·         Requested by the patient

·         The patient cannot comprehend or respond to basic questions in English

·         You are experiencing difficulty understanding your patient or your patient can only respond in a limited way

·         The patient relies on family or friends to translate

·         The patient prefers to speak in their own language

·         The patient speaks English as a second language and is in a stressful, complex or unfamiliar situation.

Always err on the side of caution when assessing whether an interpreter is needed.

Determining the Level of English Proficiency

To determine a patient’s level of English language proficiency, you may ask the following:

·         Why are you here today?

·         Is English your first language?

·         In which country were you born?

·         How long have you lived in Australia?

·         How long have you been learning or speaking English?

If the patient’s responses are difficult to understand or they cannot respond fluently, an interpreter should be booked.

Determining the Patient’s Preferred Language

A patient’s country of birth cannot be reliably used to determine their preferred language and dialect. To determine a patient’s preferred language, you may:

1.    Ask for their preferred language and dialect, if the patient speaks sufficient English.

2.    Use visual aids that list languages and dialects so that the patient can point to the language they speak.

3.    Contact a language service provider to assist you in identifying the language through a telephone interpreter.

What if an Interpreter is Refused? 

If a patient refuses the offer of an interpreter, you should:

·         Address the patient’s concerns (e.g. they may think there will be a charge)

·         Discuss the risks associated with misunderstandings or miscommunication

·         Inform them that engaging an interpreter is of benefit to Bagwan Health as much as it is to them, and that family members can still be involved as support persons.

If the patient still refuses an interpreter, then you must document the discussions and the language support that will be provided to the patient in the patient’s medical record.

Mode of Interpreting

Interpreting services are provided in three ways:

·         Onsite (face-to-face)

·         Telephone

·         Video remote.

Where possible, the patient’s preference for an onsite, telephone or video remote interpreter should be respected.

Onsite Interpreting

Onsite interpreters attend in person and are useful for:

·         Lengthy, complex situations

·         Legally binding matters

·         Facilitating a better understanding of information by taking into account non-verbal communication such as body language.

Onsite interpreting must usually be booked in advance. Most language service providers have a minimum fee for onsite interpreting, based on a 90-minute session. In rural and regional areas the availability of onsite interpreters in some languages may be limited.

Telephone Interpreting

Telephone interpreters attend via telephone and are useful for:

·         Short, non-complex matters

·         Determining the patient’s preferred language and the nature of an enquiry before an onsite interpreter is booked

·         Accessing an interpreter in rural and regional areas, when video conferencing is not available, and in less common languages in which there are a limited number of accredited interpreters

·         When immediate assistance is required and before an onsite interpreter is booked.

As telephone interpreters cannot take into account non-verbal communication, they are not used for Auslan patients. However, calls to someone who is Deaf can be made using an ordinary handset through the National Relay Service on 133 677.

Pre-booking a telephone interpreter is not required, although this should be confirmed with the language service provider.

Video Remote Interpreting

Video remote interpreting uses video conferencing systems, laptop and/or tablets to provide face-to-face communication between a patient and an off-site interpreter.

Video remote interpreters are useful for:

·         Patient’s in rural or regional areas

·         When a local Auslan interpreter is not available

·         Where an interpreter is required at short notice.

Video remote interpreting is a potentially cost-effective alternative to onsite interpreting but requires a good internet connection and suitable equipment to provide the speed and data capacity required.

Understanding the Role of Family and Friends

There are potential ethical, professional and legal consequences and significant adverse outcomes to allowing family, friends or intimate partners to facilitate interpretation. Personally involved individuals should never be used to act in the role of an accredited interpreter as they may:

·         Provide inaccurate or inadequate interpretation as they do not have the required language competence

·         Withhold or distort information due to a lack of impartiality

·         Undermine your confidence that the necessary information is being communicated appropriately

·         Not adhere to the same standards of conduct as accredited interpreters

·         Be placed in compromising or confidential situations

·         Be upset by the experience.

Family and friends can have an important and helpful role supporting and advocating for the patient, which should be acknowledged, valued and understood as completely separate from and complementary to the role of an interpreter. Engaging a qualified interpreter enables family and friends to focus on their advocacy and support role.

Children under 18 years of age should never be asked to act in the place of an accredited interpreter or to relay information between you and a patient. It poses a number of ethical dilemmas and it is also not uncommon for minors from migrant and refugee backgrounds to be fluent in English but not necessarily in their parents’ first language or languages.

Lastly, in some instances using a family member to act in the role of an interpreter may jeopardise the safety of the patient (e.g. in the case of family violence).

Documenting the Need for an Interpreter

The need for an interpreter should be clearly and visibly documented in the patient management system. Information should include:

·         Whether an interpreter was provided when requested or identified as needed

·         The patient’s preferred language

·         The patient’s preferred gender and/or religion of the interpreter, if applicable.

This information should be used to alert colleagues of the need to request an interpreter for all future consultations.

Booking an Interpreter

The following information will be required when booking an interpreter:

·         Patient’s name

·         Language/dialect required

·         Preferred gender and/or religion of the interpreter (if relevant)

·         Date and time the interpreter is required – allow time to brief the interpreter beforehand

·         Type of appointment

·         Address

·         Name and telephone contact details of the staff member who will be conducting the session

·         Nature of the matter to be discussed

·         Anticipated length of the session

·         The interpreter’s name, if a specific interpreter is required for continuity of care reasons.

For some patients, the gender and religion of the interpreter will be important. Prior to booking an interpreter, you should ask the patient if he or she has a preference.

Knowing the name of the interpreter prior to the session is also useful in identifying any concerns the patient or interpreter may have.

If booking a telephone interpreter, inform the language service provider about the telephone system that will be used e.g. is it a speakerphone, or will you and patient be using a dual handset telephone?

Requests for a Preferred Interpreter

The use of a patient’s preferred interpreter ensures that the patient is comfortable with and trusts the interpreter, and helps the communication process. This is particularly important for ongoing or sensitive sessions. Requests for a preferred interpreter can be made at the time of booking. Preferences will be observed as long as the interpreter is available and has the required professional level qualification for the situation.

If an Interpreter is not Available

In the event that an interpreter is not available, you are responsible for assessing the risks of proceeding with the session without an interpreter as opposed to the risk of rescheduling the appointment to allow time to engage an interpreter.

In case of an emergency and when an interpreter is not available, this must be noted in the patient’s record and an interpreter should be engaged as soon as possible to ensure accurate information is communicated.

Preparing for the Session

Prior to the commencing the session, brief the interpreter on general background information (e.g. the nature of the consultation), specific terms to be used (e.g. medical words) and what needs to be achieved. Depending on the duration of the session, you may also consider setting breaks for long sessions.

If the session is being conducted onsite, you must ensure the room is set up appropriately.

Consideration should be given to appropriate lighting, glare from windows and seating arrangements. Ideally, seats will be arranged in a triangle with the patient facing you and the interpreter being next to the patient.

Avoid leaving the interpreter alone with the patient, either in the room where the session will take place or in a waiting room.

If the session is being conducted via telephone or video remote, you must ensure you have access to the appropriate technology and understand how to work the telephone/IT system. Telephone interpreting is more effective when a landline is used rather than a mobile phone. It is also recommended that a telephone with a speakerphone (or two handsets) be used where possible.

Working with Interpreters

Interpreters relay the messages uttered by all parties as accurately as possible, without adding or omitting content or attempting to correct the person’s style or grammar. This includes maintaining the person’s tone of voice, style and manner of speech when interpreting into English, as well as maintaining the register of all parties’ utterances.

Do not request or expect interpreters to:

·         Assess any of the patient’s functional abilities, except for their linguistic abilities

·         Make a judgment as to the competence of the patient or establish the patient’s understanding

·         Act as a chaperone for clinical examinations

·         Act as a professional with bicultural or bilingual skills, a carer or a health advocate for the patient.

 

If the interpreter recognises cross-cultural misunderstanding, or comprehension or cognitive difficulties on the part of the patient, the interpreter may raise it with you to allow you to take appropriate steps, such as rephrasing, clarifying or asking further questions.

 

 

Working with Auslan Interpreters

 

As with all interpreting, you should speak directly to the patient and not the interpreter.

 

Auslan interpreters work in a similar way to other language interpreters. The interpreter will typically sit or stand next to the service provider and opposite the patient. This allows the Deaf person to maintain eye contact with the speaker, read body language and engage with the person speaking whilst receiving the message from the interpreter.

 

Two interpreters may take turns in signing, depending on the length of the session.

 

It is common for Deaf people to request a specific interpreter or agency, as generally Deaf people are familiar and work regularly with Auslan interpreters. This request should be accommodated where possible.

 

 

 

During the Session

At the start of the session:

·         Introduce yourself and the interpreter to the patient

·         Explain the role of the interpreter will interpret what is being said and that they are bound by confidentiality and must maintain impartiality

·         Explain the purpose of the session and what you hope to achieve

·         Do not assume that the patient knows what the session is about

·         Explain to the patient that questions or concerns can be raised at any time during the interview.

During the session:

·         Talk directly to the patient, not the interpreter, and maintain eye contact, and appropriate facial expressions and body language.

·         Use the first person when speaking to your patient. For example, say “When did you eat last?” instead of “When did she eat last?”

·         Speak clearly and use plain English. Explain complex concepts or terminology and avoid using slang, jargon, acronyms, colloquialisms and metaphors.

·         Speak at a reasonable speed and make one point at a time. Pause at the end of a sentence and avoid overlapping speech, so as to provide time for the interpreter to understand and remember what is being said and to interpret in stages.

·         Allow the interpreter to clarify information with you – if there is a need to clarify, ask the interpreter to explain this to the patient first.

·         Allow the patient to ask questions or raise issues at any time.

·         if you have any questions about the patient’s cultural background, ask the patient directly and not the interpreter.

·         In a multidisciplinary team consultation, take turns and allow adequate pauses to facilitate good quality and accurate interpretation.

·         Summarise the discussion occasionally to ensure understanding.

·         Do not ask the interpreter to edit your information to suit the patient’s background.

·         When working with a telephone interpreter, use a speakerphone or a hands-free telephone.

·         When working with a telephone or video interpreter, interact directly with the patient and ensure they manage turn-taking, and use adequate descriptive language.

At the end of the session:

·         Summarise key points for the patient

·         Check that the patient understands any information you have conveyed and if there are any final questions

·         Allow the interpreter to leave separately from the patient.

After the session:

·         Debrief the interpreter and discuss any issues experienced during the session that relate to the role of the interpreter

·         Raise any unprofessional or unsatisfactory practices directly with the interpreter

·         Do not ask for or allow the interpreter to express an opinion about the patient or what they have said.

Complaints and Feedback

If there are issues with the performance of an interpreter, discuss with the interpreter in the first instance. If not resolved, contact the relevant language service provider to make a formal complaint.

Other issues such as the interpreter not attending, charging incorrect fees or interpreters with inappropriate levels of accreditation, can also be discussed with the language service provider.

Translation Services

Translating is a specialised skill that involves the written communication of the meaning of a source-language text to an equivalent target-language text. Translated information is a great way to communicate with patients, their families and carers, and provide them with information that they can refer to later. Translated materials do not replace the need for interpreting services.

Translation services are used to translate patient-specific information, such as medical documents, and also to distribute health and service information to a broader community audience for information and educational purposes.

Prior to Translation

When the intent is to distribute health and service information to a broader community, it is integral to ensure the resource meets the needs of the service area, meets timelines, remains within budget, avoids duplication and is delivered to a high standard. This can be done by identifying planning and consultation.

Use multiple data sources such as the Australian Bureau of Statistics, Census data, recent settlement data, and service usage data to identify your target audience and gain an accurate picture of the diversity in the community.

Preferred Language

Consult with your target audience to determine their preferred language and level of literacy. In some countries, several languages may be spoken and it is important to determine which one is preferred by the local migrant community. Dialect and regional variations should also be considered when selecting language/s for translation.

In addition, consult with your target audience regarding the appropriate writing system for the target language/s. Differing writing systems may be used within particular languages e.g. some Chinese languages use traditional characters whilst others use simplified character sets.

Other Communication Options

Written translation should be avoided for communities where the majority of members have low literacy levels, e.g. refugees and asylum seekers may not be able to read or write as a result of limited or disrupted education opportunities.

Alternative ways of providing multilingual information can include:

·         Information sessions, seminars or presentations using accredited interpreters

·         Audio information, such as podcasts, CDs or DVDs, or recorded messages

·         Storyboards, including images, photos, diagrams or charts

·         Easy English, which uses clear, simple language and possibly diagrams to make information as simple as possible without changing the meaning.

Use consultation methods to discover the communication preferences of your target audience and the best way for them to disseminate your information. This can include asking focus groups, other organisations who work with the community, local committees and community groups.

Avoiding Duplication

As a guiding principle and to avoid duplication, translated resources should be shared across organisations and services. Before making a decision to translate, check available translation directories or other organisations’ websites to ensure a similar resource does not already exist.

If it does not, contact other organisations and explore developing the resource together. By sharing the cost, organisations can often develop a more comprehensive resource.

Writing for Translation

Once you have identified the message to be conveyed and confirmed that translated material is the best way to communicate that message, it’s important to prepare the text as the source content will rarely be suitable for direct translation.

The following tips will assist in preparing a text for translation: 

·         Clarity

o   Use plain English

o   Write in the active voice

o   Explain unfamiliar concepts and complex terms

o   Do not use idioms, metaphors, acronyms, professional jargon, slang, colloquialisms, euphemisms and figures of speech.

·         Brevity

o   Keep it short

o   Consider a summary for translation rather than the full publication.

·         Appropriateness

o   Adapt the source text to each community group

o   Consider the level of pre-existing knowledge in the target group

o   Be alert to cultural sensitivities about particular topics, words, images or graphics

o   Consult the community about the most appropriate way to deal with the topic.

·         Accuracy

o   Proofread the text prior to submitting it for translation and ensure it is final

o   Assume the translator will translate everything as provided – they will not be responsible for correcting errors

o   Use an editor to ensure the clarity and accuracy of the source text.

Arranging a Translation

Before the language service provider can provide a quote for the translation, they will need to know:

·         Name of the organisation

·         Purpose of the translation

·         The audience including ethnic community, age and gender

·         How the translated material will be published or broadcast

·         Any technical requirements such as the computer operating system and software.

·         Additional information including deadlines and copyright arrangements, if applicable.

Once you have engaged a translating service, the translator will require:

·         The text that will be translated, including a glossary of key terms

·         The desired languages (including dialects) for translation

·         The required accreditation level specialisation of the translator

·         The need for the translation to be typeset

·         Translation of the glossary of key terms for future reference

·         Certification of the translation if required

·         Confidentiality requirements

·         Any elements of the text that do not need to be translated (such as logo, names).

Finalising the Translation

All translations must be independently checked by a different translator with at least the same level of accreditation as the original translator. The language service provider can arrange this for an additional fee. Independent checking ensures quality and accuracy and involves comparing the translation with the original text.

Depending on the document, the translated resource should also be reviewed by the target community. This will help identify any particular words or expressions in the translated resource that are unclear or culturally inappropriate. Consider paying communities for their time.

Always publish online the translated version alongside the English version or print both together. This allows an English-speaking user to refer to the translated version with a non-English speaking patient.

Conduct periodic maintenance on translated materials to ensure the materials remain relevant and current. Make sure that the translated information is updated if the original English version is changed.

Lastly, assess the effectiveness of the translated publication by consulting with target communities, specifically requesting feedback on the publication, and/or conduct surveys of the target audience and relevant service providers.

Written Translations by Translators vs. Sight Translations by Interpreters

Some patients from migrant and refugee backgrounds may be unable to read or write in English but some may also be illiterate in their own language. This can make filling out forms or questionnaires very challenging.

 

On-site interpreters should not be asked to provide written translations of material or to fill out forms or questionnaires on behalf of a patient. Interpreters are not always certified as translators and thus, cannot provide official written translations of documentation. If possible, such materials should be translated in advance by a certified translator.

 

If it is necessary for a patient to fill out a written document, or for you to inform a patient of the contents of a document, you should read it to the patient through the interpreter and then complete the form according to the patient’s answers as conveyed by the interpreter.

 

When absolutely necessary, an on-site interpreter may provide sight translation of written information, thereby transferring a message written in English into a message delivered orally in another language. Sight translations must take place in your presence.

 

Sight translation should be used sparingly and only for brief documents (200 – 300 words). Interpreters should not be required to sight translate consent forms, complex medical reports or documents with extensive information on conditions, procedures, options of treatment and risks. Long, complex or technical documents are not suitable for sight translation and will need written translation.

Policy Bagwan Health requires all interpreters or translators, whether they are Australian Institute of Interpreters and Translators (AUSIT) members or not, to adhere to the AUSIT Code of Ethics and Code of Conduct . In summary, the code obliges members to: · Maintain professional detachment, impartiality, objectivity and confidentiality · Decline work beyond their competence · Strive for excellence through continuous regular professional development · Promote working conditions, relationships and an understanding of roles that facilitate collaboration and quality service delivery · Adhere to dispute resolution procedures. This policy defines the standards and processes associated with working with interpreting and translating services. It is intended to support staff at all levels to provide quality language services to patients and thereby respond to the needs of Victoria’s diverse community, including refugees and asylum-seekers, migrants and people using sign language. Procedure Interpreting Services Interpreting is a highly specialised skill involving the precise, effective and timely translation of information from one language to another. Including an interpreter in a consultation can be beneficial where the patient prefers to speak, or is more fluent, in a language other than English, or the patient’s English skills are inadequate for the consultation. Why Engage an Interpreter? Clear and effective communication underpins every aspect of good practice. It is linked to the patient’s satisfaction, adherence to instructions, and health outcomes. Ineffective communication can result in limited, delayed, inefficient care, leading to more costly treatment and intervention, as well as negatively impacting the patient’s understanding of, and trust in, the healthcare system at large. Engaging interpreters has been found to: · Decrease communication errors · Increase the patient’s comprehension · Reduce unnecessary tests and treatments · Improve clinical outcomes · Raise the quality of care to the same level as that for people without language barriers · Improve the patient’s satisfaction with understanding self-care and follow-up plans, reducing errors and better adherence to treatment · Improve the healthcare provider’s satisfaction Failure to determine the need for, and engage, an interpreter may be considered to be a breach in duty of care. Informed Consent Engaging an interpreter is essential for obtaining informed consent from patients with limited English proficiency or Deaf patients from migrant and refugee backgrounds. Consent for any procedure requires the patient to be: · Fully informed about the underlying illness or disease, the nature of the procedure, the consequences of not having the procedure, the degree of certainty about the outcome, the time for recovery and the cost · Able to raise any concerns about the risks of particular relevance to them. At a minimum, you should: · Assess the patient’s understanding of the information provided to consent to treatment, taking into consideration both the complexity of the issues and the person’s English language proficiency · Engage an interpreter for people with limited English language proficiency. Consent may not be valid if it is obtained through the person’s family members, partners or friends. Accessible Interpreter Services Patients must be informed of the interpreting services that are available to them when accessing health care, as well as collecting medications from a pharmacist and that services are: · Provided by certified interpreters · Free for the patient · Confidential. Assessing the Need for an Interpreter Whenever possible, the need for an interpreter should be determined prior to an appointment. Assessing how well a patient understands English is the first step in identifying the need for an interpreter. Even when a patient appears to have adequate English proficiency in an everyday conversation, stressful or unfamiliar situations may affect their ability to communicate effectively. In addition, the patient may have gaps in confidence and competence between understanding what is being said and being able to ask questions in English. In addition, Deaf people from migrant and refugee backgrounds will require an Auslan/English interpreter (if they use Auslan) or a Deaf and Auslan/English interpreter (if they use another sign language). You should engage an interpreter if: · Requested by the patient · The patient cannot comprehend or respond to basic questions in English · You are experiencing difficulty understanding your patient or your patient can only respond in a limited way · The patient relies on family or friends to translate · The patient prefers to speak in their own language · The patient speaks English as a second language and is in a stressful, complex or unfamiliar situation. Always err on the side of caution when assessing whether an interpreter is needed. Determining the Level of English Proficiency To determine a patient’s level of English language proficiency, you may ask the following: · Why are you here today? · Is English your first language? · In which country were you born? · How long have you lived in Australia? · How long have you been learning or speaking English? If the patient’s responses are difficult to understand or they cannot respond fluently, an interpreter should be booked. Determining the Patient’s Preferred Language A patient’s country of birth cannot be reliably used to determine their preferred language and dialect. To determine a patient’s preferred language, you may: 1. Ask for their preferred language and dialect, if the patient speaks sufficient English. 2. Use visual aids that list languages and dialects so that the patient can point to the language they speak. 3. Contact a language service provider to assist you in identifying the language through a telephone interpreter. What if an Interpreter is Refused? If a patient refuses the offer of an interpreter, you should: · Address the patient’s concerns (e.g. they may think there will be a charge) · Discuss the risks associated with misunderstandings or miscommunication · Inform them that engaging an interpreter is of benefit to Bagwan Health as much as it is to them, and that family members can still be involved as support persons. If the patient still refuses an interpreter, then you must document the discussions and the language support that will be provided to the patient in the patient’s medical record. Mode of Interpreting Interpreting services are provided in three ways: · Onsite (face-to-face) · Telephone · Video remote. Onsite Interpreting Onsite interpreters attend in person and are useful for: · Lengthy, complex situations · Legally binding matters · Facilitating a better understanding of information by taking into account non-verbal communication such as body language. Onsite interpreting must usually be booked in advance. Most language service providers have a minimum fee for onsite interpreting, based on a 90-minute session. In rural and regional areas the availability of onsite interpreters in some languages may be limited. Telephone Interpreting Telephone interpreters attend via telephone and are useful for: · Short, non-complex matters · Determining the patient’s preferred language and the nature of an enquiry before an onsite interpreter is booked · Accessing an interpreter in rural and regional areas, when video conferencing is not available, and in less common languages in which there are a limited number of accredited interpreters · When immediate assistance is required and before an onsite interpreter is booked. As telephone interpreters cannot take into account non-verbal communication, they are not used for Auslan patients. However, calls to someone who is Deaf can be made using an ordinary handset through the National Relay Service on 133 677. Pre-booking a telephone interpreter is not required, although this should be confirmed with the language service provider. Video remote interpreters are useful for: · Patient’s in rural or regional areas · When a local Auslan interpreter is not available · Where an interpreter is required at short notice. Video remote interpreting is a potentially cost-effective alternative to onsite interpreting but requires a good internet connection and suitable equipment to provide the speed and data capacity required. Engaging a qualified interpreter enables family and friends to focus on their advocacy and support role. pages.title: Mandatory reporting
pages.html:
Policy Number

Version Number

Scope

This policy applies to all staff and contractors employed by Bagwan Health, Allied Health professionals, Credentialed Specialists, volunteers and students.

Policy

This policy has been developed, in conjunction with the Department of Health and Human Services (DHHS) Responding to Allegations of Physical or Sexual Assault Policy, the Victorian Child Safe Standards, the Victorian Reportable Conduct Scheme and the Australian Health Practitioner Regulation Agency (AHPRA) Guidelines for Mandatory Notifications.

The goal of this policy is to provide Bagwan Health staff, contractors, volunteers and students with information to assist them in managing and reporting allegations of physical or sexual assault/abuse and in making mandatory notifications under the Health Practitioner Regulation National Law.

Procedure

Allegations of Assault/Abuse

All allegations of physical or sexual assault/abuse at Bagwan Health must be reported to the Police, whether it is a staff member or a patient, and even if the victim has not consented to the matter being reported.

In addition, all allegations of assault/abuse e.g. emotional abuse, psychological abuse, physical abuse and sexual abuse, are considered a major incident, and as such need to be reported to DHHS within 24 hrs.

The following constitutes assault and/or abuse.

  • Physical assault/abuse

Which is when a person inflicts physical injury or unwanted physical contact upon a person by hitting, throwing, shaking, suffocating, strangulating, poisoning, mutilating, or assaulting with a weapon. Physical injury includes (but is not limited to) internal injuries, dislocated or broken bones, cuts, bruising, welts or burns.

  • Sexual assault/abuse 

Which is when a person uses power or authority over a person to involve the person in sexual activity. Physical force can be involved but not always. Sexual assault/abuse can involve a wide range of sexual activities including the fondling of a person’s genitals, masturbation, oral sex, vaginal or anal penetration by a penis, finger or other object and exposure of a child to pornography.

Other actions that may constitute assault/abuse includes spitting, threatening behaviour and an attempted assault.

There are also incidents that constitute assault under the law but do not cause physical injury. These may be best dealt with incident reporting rather than being reported directly to the Police e.g. one patient shoving another with no injury caused.

Indicators of a Possible Assault/Abuse

It may become apparent that an assault and/or abuse has occurred under various circumstances including:

  • A patient alleges that an assault has occurred
  • An employee, volunteer or student observes an incident
  • An employee, volunteer or student suspects that an incident has occurred,
  • e.g. a patient may be distressed and bruised, or clothes may be ripped
  • An employee, volunteer, student or visitor alleges assault by a patient
  • A patient’s behaviour changes significantly – this might include self-destructive behaviour, sleep disturbances, acting-out behaviours, being very quiet and/or withdrawn, or persistent and inappropriate sexual play
  • A patient complains of physical symptoms or symptoms appear – this might include abdominal pain, sexually-transmitted disease, or pregnancy.

Centres Against Sexual Assault (CASA)

Centres Against Sexual Assault (CASA) operate throughout Victoria and provide both crisis and ongoing counselling support to recent and past victims of sexual assault. All victims of sexual assault, whether female or male, have the right of access to CASA services.

Available CASA services include:

  • Immediate crisis counselling and support
  • Follow-up, longer-term counselling and support
  • Information regarding the victim’s options and rights within the legal system
  • Information regarding medical options, including follow-up medical treatment
  • Assistance in the management of sexually transmitted diseases and/or pregnancy arising from the assault
  • Assistance in the management of other practical consequences of the assault such as emergency housing and compensation
  • Support and information to friends and family members.

Responsibilities

If an employee, volunteer or student has a reasonable belief that an assault and/or abuse has occurred, they are responsible for informing the relevant manager as soon as possible.

The notified manager is responsible for:

  • Ensuring immediate medical assistance is arranged, if needed
  • Contacting the Police
  • Arranging for an Independent Third Person, if needed
  • Contacting the victim’s family/guardian, if the service user is under the age of 18
  • Ensuring the victim is offered counselling
  • Clearly documenting how the victim, if over the age of 18, demonstrated that they made an informed decision not to inform their family or guardian
  • Ensuring the victim does not have an enduring power of attorney and can make an informed decision, or their power of attorney is contacted.

In instances of alleged sexual assault and if the victim consents, the relevant manager is also responsible for contacting CASA. They will do this at the same time as they inform the Police of the allegation.

Reasonable Belief

A reasonable belief is formed if a person in the same position would have formed the same belief. It is based on factual information and observations. A reasonable belief is more than suspicion, there must be some objective basis for the belief, but it’s not the same as having proof and does not require certainty.

Legal Duty

Any adult who forms a reasonable belief that a sexual offence has been committed by an adult against a child under 16 has a legal duty to report that information to police. Failure to disclose the information to the police is a criminal offence. This offence is part of the Crimes Amendment (Protection of Children) Act 2014.

There are some exemptions and/or excuses to not report including where the information has already been disclosed.

There is also a mandatory requirement to report an assault to Police where the patient:

  • Is a statutory child protection service user
  • Resides in out-of-home care
  • Is a child/adult with a disability.

Child Abuse and Neglect Incidents

The Victorian Reportable Conduct Scheme requires the centralised reporting of allegations of child abuse (sexual, physical and psychological), from workers or volunteers in relevant organisations with a high level of responsibility for children. From 1 January 2018, the scheme was applied to hospitals, other disability services for children, providers of overnight camps, religious bodies and the residential facilities of boarding schools.

The reportable conduct scheme requires allegations of suspected criminal conduct to be reported to Victoria Police as the first priority and will maintain the privacy of an investigation by Victoria Police of any allegations of criminal misconduct.

To report concerns that are life-threatening, call Victoria Police on 000.

In reporting child sexual abuse to police, your identity will remain confidential unless:

  • You disclose it yourself or your consent in writing to your identity being disclosed
  • A court or tribunal decides that it is necessary in the interests of justice for your identity to be disclosed.

Bagwan Health CEO Responsibilities

The Bagwan Health CEO needs to be informed immediately of any child abuse or neglect incidents. The CEO (or a delegate) must report any allegation of reportable conduct to the Commission for Children and Young People (CCYP) within three business days of becoming aware of the allegation. It is a criminal offence for Bagwan Health CEO to fail to notify (within three business days) and update (within 30 calendar days) the CCYP about reportable allegations.

The reporting to the CCYP by the Bagwan Health CEO is in addition to all the current steps that are required to be undertaken when an allegation of child abuse (sexual, physical and psychological) or significant neglect is made.

What Should Happen

When an allegation is made, or an employee, volunteer or student becomes aware of an assault, immediate action should be taken to ensure the person’s safety and wellbeing. All action should be undertaken in a way that is respectful of the person, is culturally appropriate, and empowers them to make their own choices and decisions wherever possible.

The most senior staff member present should:

  • Assess the situation to ensure a safe environment
  • Contact the relevant manager and inform them of the situation, as soon as possible
  • Follow directions from the manager
  • Care for the victim, and give maximum support and assistance
  • Take reasonable precautions to preserve evidence and store records relating to a report of abuse/neglect securely and only permit access to authorised persons
  • Follow any directions given by Emergency Services – it may be necessary to preserve any forensic evidence.

Patients from Culturally and Linguistically Diverse Community

Where the patient uses a language other than English, an interpreter of the same sex as the patient should be arranged as soon as possible to interpret for the patient, Police and other persons involved in the process.

People from CALD communities may be reluctant to speak to an interpreter because they fear that what they say may be passed on to their local community. In this case, it is possible to request a telephone interpreter from another state or to not disclose the person’s name to the interpreter.

When using an interpreter directly, consideration should be given to arranging an interpreter who is not associated with them or their immediate cultural community.

ASA provides culturally-specific services available to victims from CALD communities.

Mandatory Notifications for Registered Health Practitioners

The National Law requires health practitioners, employers of health practitioners and education providers to report ‘notifiable conduct’ to the Australian Health Practitioner Regulation Agency (AHPRA) in order to prevent the public being placed at risk of harm.

Section 140 of the National Law defines ‘notifiable conduct’ as when a practitioner has:

  1. Practised the practitioner’s profession while intoxicated by alcohol or drugs; or
  2. Engaged in sexual misconduct in connection with the practice of the practitioner’s profession; or
  3. Placed the public at risk of substantial harm in the practitioner’s practice of the profession because the practitioner has an impairment; or
  4. Placed the public at risk of harm because the practitioner has practised the profession in a way that constitutes a significant departure from accepted professional standards.

Making a mandatory notification is a serious step and should only be taken on sufficient grounds.

Further information can be found in the AHPRA Guidelines for Mandatory Notifications.

Employee Assistance Program (EAP)

Bagwan Health is committed to maintaining a safe and healthy working environment and recognises the need to provide confidential, professional assistance for employees/volunteer’s experiencing work-related problems. This will be provided through access to an Employee Assistance Program (EAP).

pages.title: Medication safety
pages.html:
Purpose and scope

This draft describes medication safety responsibilities for the Bagwan simulation. It applies to the use of medication information in learning scenarios. It does not authorise prescribing, dispensing or administration.

Before proceeding

  • Work within your role, competence and the approved local procedure.
  • Confirm the patient identity and the current medication information provided in the scenario.
  • Check the documented allergy and adverse drug reaction history.
  • Refer discrepancies, missing information or uncertainty to the supervising clinician or pharmacist before proceeding.

Documentation and communication

Keep medication information accurate, communicate changes during transitions of care, and record the relevant observations and actions. Use the incident reporting process for a medication incident or near miss.

Approval requirements

The SME must confirm responsibilities, local escalation arrangements, required checks and documentation before this draft is used for teaching. No medicine, dose, administration instruction or checking protocol is specified here.

pages.title: Nursing and clinical handover
pages.html:
Purpose

Support a structured transfer of relevant information and responsibility during the Bagwan simulation.

Prepare the handover

Use the handover structure approved for the learning scenario. Check the patient identity against the scenario record. Gather the current situation, relevant background, observations, identified risks, pending actions and the patient's preferences.

Give and receive the handover

  • Identify who is handing over and who will accept responsibility.
  • Communicate accurate, relevant and current information in a logical order.
  • State outstanding actions, who will complete them and when they require attention.
  • Allow questions and confirm shared understanding.
  • Record the handover and clarify any information that remains uncertain.

Approval requirements

The SME must define the required identifiers, handover framework, minimum information and escalation process for each scenario. This draft is a communication framework, not an approved clinical protocol.

pages.title: OHS/WHS
pages.html:
Policy Name

Workplace Occupational Health and Safety

Policy Number

002

Owner of Policy

Dr Christina Jones, CEO

Scope

The primary focus of all activities within Bagwan Health will be the provision of excellence in service user services whilst equally maintaining a position of excellence in the management of Workplace Occupational Health and Safety.

The goal for Bagwan Health in Health and Safety is the pro-active prevention of work-related accidents, incidents, injuries and illnesses and the development and promotion of safe systems of work. Committed to ensuring, as far as is reasonably practicable, the health, safety and welfare of the working environment for its staff, volunteers, contractors and visitors to its premises.

This policy applies to all Bagwan Health employees, contractors, volunteers and visitors to Bagwan Health’s premises, to the extent it is relevant to them.

In this policy, ‘workplace’ includes working on site or off-site, attendance at a work-related conference or function, and attendance at a client or other work-related event, including retreats and social events.

 

Term and definitions

 

Authorised person

An authorised person is the relevant Manager or the Chief Executive Officer.

 

Employee

An employee is a Bagwan Health employee, volunteer or student on placement with Bagwan Health.

 

Individual

Individual refers to Bagwan Health service users, families and friends, employees, potential employees, volunteers, students and the community.

 

Service user

A service user is a child or an adult (person with a disability) or aged person who uses a Bagwan Health service.

 

Workplace

Workplace includes working on-site or off-site, attendance at a work-related conference or function, and attendance at a client or other work-related event, including retreats and social events.

Policy

Bagwan Health supports the rights of all persons covered by the policy to work in an environment that is, so far as is reasonably practicable, safe and without risks to health.

Bagwan Health is committed to the promotion of a joint and united approach to consultation and resolution of Work Health and Safety issues, with a view to improving workplace efficiency and productivity.

This will be accomplished through the ongoing development, in consultation with Bagwan Health’s Safety Representatives, of management systems and procedures designed to, so far as is reasonably practicable:

• identify, assess and control workplace hazards;

• reduce the incidence and cost of occupational injury and illness; and

• provide a rehabilitation system for those affected by occupational injury or illness.

Workplace Occupational Health and Safety statutory requirements, including regulations and codes of practice, are minimum standards and so the aim is for them to be improved upon, where practicable.

 

Procedures
Manual handling

Bagwan Health follows legislated best practice standards to help create a safe workplace. Bagwan Health refers to detailed Workplace Occupational Health and Safety procedures as set out by Worksafe Victoria’s Health and Safety guides:

WorkSafe Victoria — healthcare and hospitals safety basics

 

1. Working safely in visiting health services: A handbook for workplaces

2. A guide to designing workplaces for safer handling of people

3. Transferring people safely – a handbook for workplaces

4. Transferring people from beds and chairs – A health and safety solution

5. Transferring people for toileting and bathing – A health and safety solution

6. Assisting people who have fallen – A health and safety solution

7. Assisting people in wheelchairs – A health and safety solution

8. Moving and supporting people with a disability – A health and safety solution

9. Re-positioning people in bed – A health and safety solution

 

Health and Safety Committee

The Bagwan Health Workplace Occupational Health and Safety Committee should meet at least every three months in a year to monitor and facilitate the development and implementation of Health and Safety Systems, throughout the organisation.

Bagwan Health Designated Work Groups are:

• Respite & Recreation

• Therapy & Inclusion Services

• Accommodation & Specialist Support Services

• Child & Youth Services

• Quality, Innovation & Service Development

• People Culture & Resources

• Finance

• Support Coordination.

 

Each Designated Work Group has at least one OH&S Committee member acting as its Health and Safety Representative. The Program Manager for each Designated Work area is also required to attend the Bagwan Health OH&S Committee meetings.

Management should review the relevant legislation to determine whether a Health and Safety Committee is required for the workplace. Management should also consult with the Health and Safety Representatives and the Human Resources Department to determine if a Committee is required at their site.

Where a Health and Safety Committee is required by legislation, or where the CEO otherwise deems it necessary, Bagwan Health will establish a Health and Safety Committee.

 

Health and Safety Committee Membership

The number of Committee members will be decided and agreed by management, in consultation with employees.

Elected health and safety representatives may also be Health and Safety Committee members. At least half of the Health and Safety Committee members must be employee representatives.

Health and Safety Committee meetings are to be conducted at least every three months in a year. An agenda will be established prior to the meeting and issued to all persons attending the meeting. Minutes will be taken and forwarded to all Health and Safety Representatives, and copies shall be made available to all employees.

Bagwan Health encourages sites to invite appropriate visitors to attend the Occupational Health and Safety meetings and positively contribute.

 

Health and Safety Representative

Management must ensure that employee representatives are selected appropriately and that the Committee is established and conducted in accordance with the applicable legislation.

The Committee Representatives are required to:

• Undertake relevant training, i.e. OH&S Representative Course, to carry the role out effectively

• Be aware of the Health and Safety interests of their Designated Work Group, and represent their concerns to their relevant Manager and the Occupational Health & Safety Committee

• Attend the OH&S Committee meetings as scheduled.

 

Committee Representatives can conduct Safety Mapping, Site Safety and Vehicle or First Aid Kit Checks and participate in the consultation processes to complete Risk Assessments aiming to best manage safety issues if required.

Where required by law, or where deemed necessary, designated workgroups shall each elect a Health and Safety Representative as their elected spokesperson.

Health and Safety Representatives are encouraged to work with management to discuss Work Health and Safety issues and to work with management to improve health and safety standards.

 

Dissemination of Policy and Procedure

The Workplace Occupational Health & Safety Policy and related procedures will be displayed in the workplace and all employees and volunteers will be provided with a copy by their supervisor/manager.

New employees will be provided with a copy of the documents as part of their induction.

The policy and related procedures will be reviewed on an annual basis or more frequently, if required, to ensure continued compliance with the relevant legislation.

 

Breach of Workplace Occupational Health and Safety Policy

Any breach of this policy may result in counselling and/or disciplinary action, which, in the case of employees, may lead to dismissal, or, in the case of volunteers, may lead to the cessation of their engagement.

Any breach of this policy by a contractor may result in the cancellation by Bagwan Health of the services provided by that contractor.

 

Roles and responsibilities

Bagwan Health acknowledges that the active cooperation of all managers, employees, volunteers’ students and service users is required for ensuring a safe and healthy working environment. Consequently, the management of Bagwan Health is committed to a consultative approach to Workplace Occupational Health and Safety.

All Bagwan Health employees, volunteers and students are expected to contribute to the improvement of health and safety within the workplace and to help facilitate cooperation on health and safety issues and to ensuring health and safety measures are implemented.

 

CEO and other executives

The CEO and other executive officers will:

• be committed to the provision and maintenance of a healthy and safe workplace

• consult and participate in the health and safety program

• use risk identification, assessment and control principles to reach Bagwan Health’s health and safety objectives

• inform and train all persons to whom this procedure applies in relevant policies, procedures and health and safety obligations

• participate in Bagwan Health’s inductions and implement all safety procedures.

 

Human Resources

The Human Resources Department will:

• be committed to the provision and maintenance of a healthy and safe workplace

• ensure that all staff receive the appropriate training in the policy and related procedures, and their obligations under occupational health and safety laws.

 

Supervisors and Managers

Supervisors/managers will:

• be committed to the provision and maintenance of a healthy and safe workplace

• consult and participate in the health and safety program

• use risk identification, assessment and control principles to reach Bagwan Health’s health and safety objectives

• inform and train all staff in relevant policies, procedures and health and safety obligations

• participate in Bagwan Health inductions and implement all safety procedures.

 

Employees

Employees will: 

• participate in health and safety training, actions and activities and support Bagwan Health in its efforts to reach its health and safety and, where relevant, rehabilitation objectives

• follow reasonable health and safety instructions from managers or supervisors;

• report any serious incidents, accidents, injuries or hazards in the workplace to supervisors or designated representatives

• aim to work in a way that does not endanger the health or safety of themselves or others

• properly use and maintain safety equipment

• make sure visitors follow safety rules in the workplace

• participate in Bagwan Health induction programs and implement all detailed safety procedures

• assess risks to their health and safety arising from the provision of their service

• have control measures in place to address those risks, including complying with any relevant Bagwan Health policies and practices.

 

Health and Safety Committee

The role of the Health and Safety Committee is to:

• assist in the development, monitoring and review of health and safety policies and procedures

• consider any proposal for, or changes to the workplace, policies, work practices or procedures which may affect the health and safety of employees

• promote the importance of health and safety amongst management and employees

• monitor Bagwan Health’s health and safety performance

• monitor the rehabilitation of injured employees

• assist in the resolution of health and safety disputes.

The Committee will meet on a quarterly basis, or more frequently if required. An agenda will be circulated by the Head of the Committee prior to the meeting. A sample agenda can be found in Appendix B to this procedure. A designated note-taker will take minutes of the meeting. A sample minutes document can be found in Appendix A to this procedure. 

 

Health and Safety Representatives

The role of Health and Safety Representatives is to:

• represent employees from their workgroup in relation to health and safety matters

• investigate health and safety-related complaints prior to representations to management

• make representations to management and report back to employees on any matter relating to health and safety

• discuss with the employees, any proposals or matters which may affect the health and safety of employees

• assist management in the identification of hazards, the assessment of risks and implementation of risk control measures

• assist in promoting adherence to health and safety policies and procedures

• assist in the monitoring of risk controls and health and safety policies and procedures.

 

Forms and templates

Please refer to the following forms and templates:

• Sample Minutes – Health and Safety Committee Meeting

• Sample Agenda – Health and Safety Committee Meeting
